common_name: Aromi Sunstruck Azalea (Fragrant Lemon-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; give it room to reach its mature upright size before crowding it with companion shrubs.

directions: Bred by Dr. Eugene Aromi of Mobile, Alabama by crossing Rhododendron austrinum with the Knap Hill hybrid 'White Swan,' Aromi Sunstruck combines the native species' Gulf Coast heat tolerance with a refined, wavy-edged lemon-yellow flower borrowed from its English parent. Pale yellow buds open in mid-to-late spring into fragrant, tubular blooms roughly two inches across, covering the upright shrub before or as the leaves emerge. It reaches a narrow, upright habit noticeably taller than wide, making it useful as a woodland-edge accent rather than a spreading foundation shrub. Plant in humus-rich, acidic soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid heavy pruning since flower buds set on the previous year's growth.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas

common_name: Aromi Sunrise Azalea (Fragrant Golden Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; the informal, layered branching benefits from an open site rather than tight foundation spacing.

directions: Introduced in 1987 by Mobile, Alabama hybridizer Dr. Eugene Aromi from a cross of the Knap Hill hybrid 'Hiawatha' with the native Rhododendron austrinum, Aromi Sunrise carries large, sweetly fragrant flowers in brilliant yellow lit by a vivid orange-yellow blotch. Its softly spreading, informally layered habit sets it apart from the more upright growth of many native azalea hybrids, giving it a graceful presence at a woodland edge or shrub border. It flowers heavily in spring before or as new leaves emerge and shows the strong heat and humidity tolerance typical of Aromi's austrinum-derived breeding line. Grow in consistently moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade for best performance through Gulf South summers.

common_name: High Tide Azalea (Fragrant Ivory Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; this is one of the larger-growing Aromi hybrids and needs generous space at maturity.

directions: High Tide is one of the larger-flowered native azalea hybrids bred by Dr. Eugene Aromi of Mobile, Alabama, producing delicate ivory blooms brightened by a golden blotch and a light pink flush at the petal tips. The fragrant flowers open in a heavy spring flush on a vigorous, upright-growing shrub that reaches taller than most Aromi introductions at maturity. Like other hybrids in this breeding line, it draws its Gulf Coast heat and humidity tolerance from native austrinum-group parentage crossed with large-flowered Exbury-type azaleas. Site it in humus-rich, acidic soil with dappled woodland light, and mulch well to keep the shallow roots cool and evenly moist through summer.

common_name: Tipsy Tangerine Azalea (Fragrant Orange Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; avoid heavy pruning since flower buds form on the previous season's wood.

directions: Bred by Dr. Eugene Aromi of Mobile, Alabama, Tipsy Tangerine opens rich scarlet buds into fragrant flowers that fan through several shades of orange around a deep yellow blotch, a warm color range distinct from the more common yellow and pink Aromi selections. The upright shrub blooms in early to mid-spring on wood set the previous season, and its native-derived heat and humidity tolerance makes it a reliable performer where Asian and Exbury-type azaleas often struggle. Grow it in humus-rich, evenly moist, acidic soil at a partly shaded woodland edge, and mulch to conserve the moisture deciduous native azaleas need through summer dry spells.

common_name: Glory Be Azalea (Large-Trussed Fragrant Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade; this is one of the largest-growing Aromi hybrids and needs a spacious woodland-edge site rather than a tight foundation bed.

directions: Glory Be combines three southeastern native species — Rhododendron prunifolium, R. viscosum, and R. arborescens — crossed with the Exbury-type 'Rufus' by Mobile, Alabama breeder Dr. Eugene Aromi, and reportedly took its name from a visitor's exclamation on first seeing the shrub in bloom. It produces unusually large, fragrant, bright yellow trusses with a deep yellow blotch on a vigorous shrub that grows substantially larger than most native azalea hybrids, reflecting the size of its late-blooming R. prunifolium parent. Its mixed-species heritage extends bloom season later into early summer compared with the earlier-flowering austrinum-based Aromi hybrids. Give it a spacious, humus-rich, consistently moist woodland site with filtered light, since crowding or dry shade will stunt the enormous flower trusses this cultivar is grown for.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Red Whisk Azalea (Fragrant Lemon-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea with Scarlet Stamens)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; this later-blooming selection extends native azalea color into early summer.

directions: Bred by Dr. Eugene Aromi from a cross of the southeastern natives Rhododendron arborescens and R. cumberlandense, Red Whisk pairs light lemon-yellow petals with long, bright scarlet stamens that project well beyond the small, roughly one-and-a-half-inch flowers, giving each bloom the fine, brush-like accent the name describes. Because both parent species flower later than R. austrinum, Red Whisk extends the native azalea season into late spring and early summer on a medium-sized, well-branched shrub. It shares its parents' preference for consistently moist, acidic soil and tolerates more open, sunnier sites than many Aromi selections descended from shade-loving austrinum. Mulch well and avoid letting the shallow root zone dry out, especially through the first two growing seasons.
sources: Azalea Society of America — Aromi Deciduous Azaleas
Journal American Rhododendron Society, v56n1 — The Aromi Azaleas

common_name: Dancing Rabbit Azalea (Fragrant Golden-Yellow Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; its compact, upright habit fits smaller woodland-edge beds better than many larger Aromi hybrids.

directions: Dancing Rabbit was bred by Dr. Eugene Aromi of Mobile, Alabama by crossing two of his own earlier golden-flowered introductions, 'Appalachian Gold' and 'Goldstrike,' producing deep yellow buds that open into bright, fragrant yellow flowers with a deep yellow blotch. Its compact, upright growth habit is more restrained than many Aromi hybrids, packing full, rounded flower clusters onto a shrub sized for smaller garden spaces. Like its parents, it carries the Gulf Coast heat and humidity tolerance that native austrinum-derived breeding brings to the Knap Hill and Exbury azalea lines. Give it moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in dappled shade, and expect the fragrant blooms and their visiting bees and hummingbirds to peak in early to mid-spring.

common_name: Appalachian Gold Azalea (Fragrant Large-Flowered Golden Native Hybrid Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade to morning sun; this parent cultivar of 'Dancing Rabbit' grows larger than its compact offspring.

directions: One of Dr. Eugene Aromi's foundational golden-flowered introductions, Appalachian Gold bears large, fragrant blooms in a rich golden yellow deepened by a bold gold blotch, later used as a parent for the more compact 'Dancing Rabbit.' The shrub grows into a larger, more open habit than its offspring, producing a heavy spring flush of trusses before or as the leaves emerge. Its name reflects the golden color of the flowers rather than any specific place of origin, distinguishing it from wild Appalachian species like R. calendulaceum despite the naming echo. Plant in humus-rich, acidic, evenly moist soil at a woodland edge with dappled light, and mulch to protect the shallow root system through Gulf South summers.
